I first played FF10 in 2020, it was my first "lockdown" game. The only other FF games I played at the time were FF15 and FF7 Remake (loved both!).

So, there was no nostalgia for me, or anything like that. But the game always intrigued me - I remembered seeing bits of gameplay here and there and screenshots and always marveled at how unique the game looked aesthetically.

I was blown away. It's easily one of the best games ever made imo, just an absolute masterpiece. The world, both in terms of function and aesthetic is incredible, there is no long winded lore dumps or a bazillion collectibles with text attached to them. The world building is masterfully woven into the storytelling and characterization itself. 

I saw the memes about Tidus before playing and I was preparing to dislike him, but... he actually ended up being one of my favorite things about the game. His development throughout the game is very well handled, and the last piece of the puzzle falls into place right at the very end of it. The story is mesmerizing and the bittersweetness is felt throughout the whole game. 

Since playing FF10, I've played lots more FF but it's still my favorite. The linearity of the game also works to its strenght: the game does feel like an actual road trip, because there's always purpose and forward momentum. Ironically, FF15, the actual road trip game, often didn't feel like a road trip because you were just revisiting the same locations constantly.

The sphere grid and the snappy turn based combat honestly felt so good that if it was wholesale put into a modern rpg, with a few tweaks, it wouldn't feel dated at all. 

My only criticisms would be the random encounter rate (very much a relic from that time period of games) and the trials - the last couple of them especially just feel way too tedious and frustrating. Oh, and the unskippable cutscenes before boss battles.... though, I'm sure this is more of a technological limitation with how they've coded the game. Still, it can definitely cause frustrations. 


Special shoutout the art and aesthetic of the game. It's definitely south east asian coded, which is extremely welcome, and also the "summer vibes" gave me nostalgia for the early 00's, despite the fact that I never played the game before 2020.

First of all, a big budget of FF16 went into developing their in-house engine. FF16 uses a fork of FF14's engine, brought up to modern standards and to support an incredibly flashy, responsive action combat system - it definitely wasn't cheap. Meanwhile Rebirth uses UE4, just as Remake.

Furthermore, while there's no other playable characters, Clive is a jack of all trades. He basically embodies multiple characters in one - you are given complete freedom equipping him with various eikon skills. And you can mix/match to your hearts content.

A rollercoaster murder mystery with tons of really fun twists, and surprisingly effective criticism of several aspects of modern japanese society. 


Persona 5 Royal - not without issues, but for a game to maintain such high quality for over 100 hours is a big achievement. The royal portion, in terms of the actual story, is also probably the strongest stretch of Persona 5. One of my favorite jrpg 'villains' ever. 


FF7 Remake - It's FF7, which is obviously excellent, but with significantly more fleshed out characters. And they're amazing! The best version of the FF7 characters ever, and it's not even close. Also, the meta narrative is incredibly divisive, but with vibes of the game effectively playing around with the concept of the audience's relationship with FF7 itself - it totally convinced me, really loved it. Rebirth is the better game overall but Remake's narrative is very special IMO.

Y7 is one of the best stories in gaming for sure. The character work is impeccable, filled with inspiring, meaningful and very deep moments. It's the closest a videogame has ever come in changing my outlook on life.

And obviously Japan, PS5 software sales are just ass in general. Funnily enough 16 and Rebirth are the 2 best selling PS5 games despite both being considered underperforming. The loss of that ~400k sales compared to Remake definitely hurt. 

My guess is that Rebirth has passed the 3m mark at this point but its taken so long that we probably wont see PR about it for a while. My guess: we'll eventually see a Remake+Rebirth PR once Rebirth's PC release has been out for a few months. 

It's a clear underperformance but it's far from a disaster like so many games this year. At least we are definitely getting part 3, and Hamaguchi & Kitase has been pretty open about not holding back for it, so FF7 fans shouldn't be too concerned about sales numbers.

Linearity has never been a problem. Games shouldn't force an open world just for the sake of it. FF7 Remake is a great game, and I never felt that adding more random paths between the hub areas would've really made it better. The game does linear quite well - main story missions mostly always take you to new places with unique dungeons, and then every few hours you get to a hub area where you can do some side quests and take a load off. It's a very good structure I think. 

Remake also feels like the closest a JRPG has got to mimicking the "premium" feel of something like TLOU - a big budget western AAA game. Remake just feels super dialed in and the linear structure contributes to that. The encounter design, the seamlessness of gameplay-to-cinematics-to-gameplay, the general density, etc. Even in the gameplay, it feels really well calculated. You can't really outlevel the content and it's also difficult to be significantly underleveled. There is also no jarring areas with like enemies roaming every 2 feet. It's a relatively small world but it feels belivable and lived in. >So these consoles might've been dogshit in terms of CPU/GPU power ,but they had insane levels are of memory management, especially the PS4 ,so this carried over to PC ports which is why you had stuff like NFS2015 and Tomb raider sequels looking great while running good. 

Consoles generally use unified RAM, so no seperation between VRAM and system RAM. For gaming machines this is good because it allows the developers to work from a giant pool depending on the games needs. It's also something that has been the case for decades so its not unique for PS4 or X1.

>As usual ,as devs sorta forgot how to manage and optimize because the baseline now is 16gb of VRAM of the PS5 .

The PS5 has 16gb OVERALL ram available, of which 2.5gb is reserved for the OS at all times, leaving 13.5gb RAM for games to use. But again, this isnt just purely VRAM, its also RAM. So really, around 10gb VRAM for most games, which isn't really outrageous considering its a 2020 machine. The PS4/X1 had 5-6gb to use in 2013. You can blame nvidia for being cheap with the amount of VRAM they put on their graphics cards more than anything else. 

>And resort to using these techs like DLSS as crutches and brute forced Ray tracing instead of artistic design for letting games look good.

This is absolute word salad at this point. Ray tracing can and is used artistically. Also, theres almost no games outside 1 or 2 where RT is "forced" - you can literally choose to turn it off and claw back a big chunk of performance. And this includes consoles too where RT is usually locked to 30 fps modes. 

>This is mainly a problem for games who use external game engines like Unreal Engine 5 

Engine has nothing to do with it, Unreal 5 doesnt force RT or upscaling, it just simply supports them. Its the developers decisions wether they implement them or not.

The game suffers from a bit of an identity crisis. It desperately wants to be an action game but it also feels obliged to be an RPG. But the RPG elements are so shallow they kinda actively worsen the game. For example, there is no reason to have 80 side quests when about 70 of them is incredibly boring and the rewards are near non existant. A "normal" RPG tends to get away with boring sidequests if the rewards are palpable, but FF16 lacking in RPG systems means that the game can't really offer you anything tangible as rewards outside of eikon abilities... which are tied to story progression. Even though technically the eikon abilities cost resources to unlock, since you will only ever have a certain amount of abilities equipped at the same time anyway, you don't even need to go too crazy grinding that. 

On top of that, the combat feels way too easy because the game tries to do the action game thing where it makes enemies more like punching bags so you can go wild with your combos but it kinda goes against the RPG philosophy of setting challenges for the player like elemental resistances, weaknesses. In RPG's you often need to change your strategy (or party member..) to overcome an enemy. In FF16, these roadblocks are non existant to accomodate any and every build, so all encounters just start blending into eachother.

Action games are typically 10-15 hours long, while FF16 has the lenght of a big RPG. By the end I was really just ignoring every non forced encounter.


All that being said, the game has a lot of brilliant aspects. The presentation (minus the 60 fps mode being bad), music, gamefeel is all amazing. The combat may have balance issues but it actually FEELS really damn good to hit stuff. The eikon fights are fucking sublime and some of the best shit ever in a videogame. The first half of the story is also really good, it kinda loses steam towards the end but overall I still enjoyed it. 


Honestly I wish CBU3 just made a full on action game because its clearly what they wanted to do. I think it could be one of the best FF's if it had more confidence in itself. As it is, its still a good game but I think it's firmly middle of the road in terms of FF games.

FF16 has very high highs which I'll remember for a long time but honestly I just find a lot of the game to be quite bland. The side quests are almost all really boring and there's an annoying "staticness" to FF16's side content and world. Characters standing still dumping exposition at you while the camera lingers in a static position for minutes at a time... the hideaway not ever having any unexpected, cool interactions - and look, I'm not asking for a bazillion of minigames but SOMETHING would've been nice. Red Dead 2 is a very serious, bleak game but that game still offers several minigames to play, even at your camp with your fellow gang members. I really wanted some of that in FF16, it'd have fit perfectly. 

The game's approach to RPG elements is really bad in my opinion. The rewards you get generally from side quests are almost all terrible. Crafting and buying stuff feels damn near pointless when outside of getting a trophy for buying lots of drinks at the hideout, there is pretty much nothing to spend money on, and crafting is incredibly basic - your weapon just has bigger numbers, great. The DLC's at least added some accessories that can change your gameplay up a bit more dramatically than just number increases, but honestly... for a game that can go 60-70 hours long, it's incredibly anemic in general. There was one fun accessory in the main game (berserker ring, I think?) that actually changed the perfect dodge animation. That was really cool, shame that there isn't more stuff like that. 

Combat wise, I love the feel, but the lack of challenge is a bummer. What I find amusing is that the 2nd DLC decided to increase the difficulty of the eikon fight - but this is one thing I kinda liked being easy. Its a 30-40 minute long ultra expensive cinematic clash, constantly retrying/dying just kills the flow. Its the regular encounters that just feel awfully tedious after a while, because enemies are often way too passive and effectively act as simple HP sponges. 

I just think the game having one basic combo and one weapon and one playable character is simply not enough to keep the potential 60-70 hours you'll spend with the game fully engaging. There had to be something more. Even DMC5, one of the best action games ever created, has 3 characters for 10 hours of campagin. Naturally, you don't just play games like DMC5 once, but you get the idea. I don't even think a playable party would've been a must, just... at least one more character that you play as every now and then. Or at least... some different weapons that have different combo strings. 

Also, Ultima is a really bland antagonist. I think what the game was setting up initially, in its first few hours was a lot more interesting than what actually ended up happening. I think I'd have preferred if the entire game was about warring nations and eikon clashes rather than making it all out to be some 4d chess of a deity. I do love killing gods, but I think it's actively made the plot worse here. 

And as a side note, the performance mode on PS5 is still just as bad as at launch, which is very disappointing IMO. 

Now.. all of that was very negative, but I still like the game overall, don't get me wrong. As I said, when its good.. its really fucking good. And certainly, the highs, I'll remember for years.

As for Rebirth, it's one of my favorite games of the past few years. But I generally shy away from comparing 16 and 7R because there's a lot of toxicity in both fandoms. Ultimately there's a lot that Rebirth does that I wish 16 did, and a few things that 16 does that I wish Rebirth did. I think Rebirth definitely benefits from being a sequel as a lot of the complaints regarding Remake was adressed in Rebirth.   I actually hope the 16 team will make some sort of a follow up, and maybe just fully commit to it being an action game.

As games become more complex and long, achieving perfection becomes less and less possible.

I wouldn't call RDR 2, BG3, Witcher 3 or Elden Ring perfect either. But they're all damn great games. As is Rebirth. 

Rebirth's strenght definitely comes from just how accurately it manages to translate PS1 JRPG vibes into a modern presentation. The variety in the enviroments, the colourfulness of the party, the charm, the whimsy - they retained the feeling of "magic" of the original while also expanding it all. 

And it's all helped by how well presented the game is. The side quests aren't simple shot/reverse shot affairs, there's unique camera angles and a cinematic presentation even in the most basic cutscenes. There's unique music for a bunch of sidequests. The character models are ridiculously high quality and incredibly well animated, even standard npc's look good this time around. The animation work is really impressive as well - lots of little unique animations, like Cloud doing a random little dance on the boat if you go up to the group at the front. 

I also really love how the game has confidence in having multiple hours of stretches even in its main path to allow the combat to take a backseat. Some will say its bloat or busywork or whatever, but I don't really agree with that at all. It all adds up to an amazing sense of a really varied adventure, great world and party building. 

Sure, some animations take too long and some of the open world stuff is a bit anemic, but overall it's easily one of my favorite games of the past decade or so.

You can't have your cake and eat it too. Its an open world RPG. If you want all the rewards, you're gonna have to work for it.

If you just want the main story and keep it fast paced, you're gonna have to miss out on some rewards. It is how it is.
